utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to resume its -- the re-examination of the witness, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, may I ask you to escort Mr. Mandic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mandic. Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic. Yes, I take it from your answer that you do hear me in a language you understand. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before doing so, I'd like to remind you, Mr. Mandic, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both the Court and I indicated yesterday that we would be brief today, and I certainly intend to do so. There are two matters I wish to raise. The first concerns discussion about conditions in Kula, and in that connection, I'd simply like to present you with a document dated 25 May 1992 from the -- bearing the heading of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Ministry of Internal Affairs, signed by Milenko Tepavkovic chief of the SJB Novi Grad. The ERN is ET 0345-5968.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I perhaps should note that this is a document that was closed to the Defence recently but is closely connected with another document. I don't believe there's any concern on the part of the Defence about this particular document, but I leave it to Mr. Stewart is if there is. It's closely related to the May 20th document already produced as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not really in a position to express any concern or lack of concern, Your Honour, but that means I'm not expressing any concern at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's a new exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I take it? So that would then get, Mr. Registrar, number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, P464 and it's English translation gets P464.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P464 was, in addition to being sent by Mr. Tepavkovic was directed to the under-secretary of the SJB for the Ministry of Internal Affairs and also to the Ministry of Justice, and particularly to the attention of the minister. I'd simply like to ask you if this is another document in which Mr. Tepavkovic identified some of the conditions that were prevailing in Kula at the time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, there was also discussion yesterday about the interest in and efforts to unify the military and civilian courts and the concern stemming from the functioning of those institutions. In connection with that, let me ask you the following: First of all, is it correct that immediately after the commencement of war operations, and then during most of the pendency of 1992, that there was a great deal of abandoned non-Serb property in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that abandoned property was the subject of concern by the authorities of Republika Srpska, and is it also correct that that property was supposed to be placed in government coffers, supposed to revert to the government of Republika Srpska, to the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into the war commodity reserves, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there concern among the authorities in Republika Srpska about the looting of this abandoned property, and therefore, the taking of that property to places other than the war commodity reserves?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you my personal opinion, since this was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior and the Army of Republika Srpska. However, there were problems with the property abandoned by the non-Serbs, and there were attempts to prevent the looting by paramilitary formations and by civilians who would make forced entry into such dwellings and steal the property found therein.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also concern, I take it, about looting by members of the army or the police in addition?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the army, especially of the police doing any looting. I believe that this had to do mostly with the paramilitary formations and Serb civilians who remained in these areas struck by the war. People, fearing poverty and shortages of food, would go to other people's dwellings or there would be paramilitary formations present in the area where property was abandoned and would commit such offences. I am not aware of any cases where the army or the police had been involved in the looting, especially in the cases where police would have been involved in any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try to be clear about it, but as quickly as possible. We're talking about property worth a tremendous amount of money; is that correct, a great deal of property and a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've tried to follow the request that was made earlier of not objecting prematurely before one sees where the questioning is going, and for a little while, I had supposed that this line of questioning was in some way closely linked to the issue of unification of civil and military jurisdiction. But so far, that hasn't become apparent. If there is not such a link, then I do ask how this arises out of cross-examination, because it doesn't appear to be sufficiently closely linked to any issue that was explored in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough, Your Honour. Let me jump to a question that will make that link quite evident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll hear your next question, and Mr. Stewart gets an opportunity to object before the witness answers the question, if he wants to, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, during 1992, did it turn out to be the case that the concern over the efforts to prosecute looting were more forcefully voiced by the authorities of Republika Srpska and given more attention by the judicial system than the efforts to prosecute crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that doesn't at all make clear where that link is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although the link is remote, it's sufficient. So you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you may repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, during 1992, did it turn out to be the case that the concern over the efforts to prosecute looting were more forcefully voiced by the authorities of Republika Srpska and given more attention by the judicial system than the efforts to prosecute crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the past couple of days, I've been trying to answer, or rather, to present the situation in the military and civilian judiciaries in the beginning of the war, before this Honourable Trial Chamber. At that time, Bosnia and Herzegovina was cut off into different regions, both in terms of communication links and roads, and I didn't know what was going on in the other parts of Bosnia except for the Sarajevo area. For this reason, I would not be able to answer your question. I was really not informed about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me give you one prominent example, if I may, and then we'll -- well, let me start there. Are you familiar with the arrest of members of the unit -- the unit known as the Yellow Wasps in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the members of the yellow wasps were released after three days?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The problem lay in the fact that these paramilitary formations from Mali Zvornik and Loznica, in Serbia, mistreated not only the non-Serb population but even the Serbs. They pulled over vehicles where there were ministers inside and would take away the vehicles, and that's why within the MUP a decision was made to engage a unit to go and arrest members of this particular unit. I don't know what happened to them later on. I believe this was in late 1992. This was a group that had criminal origin, that would mistreat both Serbs and non-Serbs, and I don't know what their fate was, but I know that Milenko Karisik was personally in charge of this particular operation that had as its mission the arrest of the members of this unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you made aware of the fact that members of the Yellow Wasps during their period of detention admitted to killings of non-Serbs in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Judges have also some questions to you, Mr. Mandic. Judge Canivell will ask his questions first. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You had said yesterday, after being asked by Mr. Tieger, that when you promoted the creation of the separate Serb police in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you operated under the instructions and orders that you had received. Can you tell us whose orders were you following, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the letter, the dispatch that I sent, that was pursuant to an order by the minister Mico Stanisic, and on the instructions of the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: And at this time, the accused, Mr. Krajisnik, was presiding this Assembly, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Krajisnik was president of the joint Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and president of the Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic, good afternoon to you. I wish to clarify two points which were noted by Defence counsel. First, the first point has to do with the relationship between government and the legislative power. You were questioned on this relationship, and you were asked whether each decision had to be confirmed or transmitted to the Assembly, and you answered "no." Now, I understand quite well that there is a certain relationship between the executive power and the legislative power. Therefore, my question is the following: In broad lines, in general, the directing lines the Assembly had or not a power, direction, power, to give directions to the government [as interpreted]? Could the Assembly direct the government --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just explain, Your Honour, who wielded the legislative and the executive branches of power in a state of imminent threat of war that existed in 1992. The legislative power was wielded by the Assembly and the president of the Assembly, who, under the constitution, had the legislative authorities of the Assembly. The executive branch was run by the government, and under the constitution, it did not have to account for its activities to the Assembly except when it had to submit a report on its activity to the Assembly at sessions that were specifically summoned to that effect. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] It followed the directions which came from the Assembly, as the representation of the people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government worked pursuant to the constitution and the laws governing the work of the different ministries. It was clearly provided for what the purview of the government was. That was provided for under the constitution and the law on the government. You knew precisely which were the competences of the government and which of the Assembly. The government was answerable for its work to the Assembly. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Responsible to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the legality of their work. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Well, so there is another question which is connected to this, which is to say about information, about your knowledge concerning the situation in the field, in particular, about the detention centres and the way the detainees were treated. You said you got information from practically everywhere that the media were reporting, and that there was contradictory information about this. My question is quite simple: Did the Republika Srpska have its own television and its own radio and newspapers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did have the television and radio broadcasts, not the newspapers. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Let's be clear about May. I'm talking about the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there was the Serbian television and radio at Pale, but Republika Srpska did not have its newspapers. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Under whose authority were the television and radio?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the government. The minister of information was in charge of the radio and television in Republika Srpska. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Right. So yourself, when you saw these broadcasts, personally you were not sure about the information, you were not trustful of the information which appeared on the screens, television in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Pale, or rather, in Sarajevo, there was a media war being waged between the warring parties. Therefore, whatever the federal television from Sarajevo broadcast, it was certainly contrary to what had been broadcast by the Pale television. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] -- television in Pale. You are responsible to the government. You said that some media were broadcasting information which were contradictory in a certain way. But as for yourself, did you trust the information which emanated, which was broadcast by the television and which was speaking in the name of the government, of your government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And on the screens of this television, nothing was said about mishandling of the detainees, was there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. If you, Your Honour, have the month of May in mind, I don't remember. We heard Ms. Plavsic discussing the problems in these facilities, but the Pale television must have broadcast news about this, and I had no reason to doubt whatever was broadcast by the Pale television. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] My following question is: If there were at least a few places where people were detained, did your government ask for monies to keep these detention places going?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those centres came under the jurisdiction of the Army of Republika Srpska, which did not belong to or come under the authority of the executive powers, the executive government. And so the budget of the army did not have to go through the government. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You said there was, for instance, in Kula, the prison was under the authority of police, and I should think that it wasn't the only place which was under the authority of the police. Did the police itself -- because if I understand well what was being said, some detainees -- there were more detainees than it would have been normal. So are you aware of the fact that the government would have requested monies for the necessary expense to have these detention places continuing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP would contact the government and then the government would allocate funds for the prison in Kula held by the police. So resources were provided, because there was a lot of fluctuation in the civilian population. There was fighting going on in the area, almost throughout the whole of 1992. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But what was the magnitude or what was the amount, rather, of these monies, of this budget? Would you quote a figure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't say, Your Honour. I don't remember. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I'll now pass to another topic. You said that Mr. Zepinic had resigned -- sent his resignation to the president of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik. In which way in -- what quality did he actually send his resignation [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic tabled his written resignation to the president of the Assembly of the Serb people, that is to say, to Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but what was his official position? Mr. Krajisnik could accept or refuse this request or resignation of Mr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic tabled his resignation to the post of deputy minister, and he tabled it to the Assembly of the Serb People. And I think Mr. Krajisnik accepted his resignation. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but normally, shouldn't a member of the government send in his resignation to the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the government hadn't been formed. There was what was called a Ministerial Council that was in place. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, indeed. So you say it was a tradition or it was indeed the case that everybody would address oneself to the president of the Assembly, it was the president of the Assembly who, if I may say, had the power to accept or refuse nomination or resignation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was disagreement between Vitomir Zepinic, on the one hand, and Mico Stanisic, on the other, who was the newly nominated minister of the Serbian MUP on the other side. And the rest of us, the other Serb cadres in the joint MUP. And we tried to solve this problem at a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, where Mico Stanisic proposed that we go to that meeting, and Mr. Krajisnik accepted to have us. And in his cabinet, in his offices, after talking to us, there were 10 to 15 of us there, members of the MUP, that is, Vitomir Zepinic tabled his resignation to the post he held up until then, and he handed over his letter of resignation to Mr. Krajisnik. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So you say that Mr. Krajisnik was the competent authority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who the competent authority was, but Mr. -- the letter of resignation was handed over to Mr. Krajisnik. The Serbian government didn't exist at that time. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] My last question has to do with the following: To your knowledge, was there any conflict, open or not, overt or covert, between the civilian power, including the party, political party, the SDS, and the army, was there any conflict between the two?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And on what basis are you affirmative when you say "yes"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the army, and especially the leadership of the army, behaved in an independent, autonomous way, voluntarily, and did not accept any proposals made by the government or the Assembly. They only had respect for the president of the Republika Srpska and communicated with him about the way in which they were going to conduct the war. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So in the army, if somebody was going to be promoted, who was competent to promote in the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the chief of the General Staff who was in charge, Mr. Ratko Mladic, at the level of general, but after that, the highest level by the president of the Republic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Alone? Was it the president of the Republic alone who had this power? So General Mladic was nominated by a decision made by the president of the Republic on his own, without consulting anybody else, without taking the opinion of anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know, but I think that General Mladic came to Bosnia as a general. He already held the rank of general, I believe. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but then the fact that he was appointed head of the army, who decided on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was appointed by the president of the Republic, but I'm not quite sure, that he was nominated as chief of the General Staff, and this was endorsed by the Assembly. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] By the Assembly? By the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be quite frank, I'm not sure of the provisions. But as far as I can remember, Ratko Mladic was appointed chief of the General Staff by the president of the Republic, that is to say, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and I'm not quite sure, but I think that was endorsed by the Assembly, or rather, whether it was or wasn't, I'm not sure, whether that came under its competence. But you have that in the rules governing the army and the rules governing the Assembly of the National Peoples Republic as well. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Well, according to you, was the army politicised? Because everybody knows that under certain regimes, a communist regime, for instance, the party had its own influence, had its way to say for nominations or promotions in the army. So to your knowledge, was the army politicised in such a way? Did the party have an influence, some influence on the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal opinion, Your Honour, is that the party, or rather, the civilian authorities, had very little influence on the army, and the army acted independently and exerted its authority as it saw fit. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm speaking of the party.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the party was equated with the civilian authorities, because all the leaders of the party were in the powers and authorities that be, officially speaking, in Republika Srpska. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So if I understand your answer, Dr. Karadzic was indeed the person who had civilian office, but power and authority on the military, on the army.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well, Mr. Mandic. You just answered to a question of Judge El Mahdi and said that the army behaved in an independent and autonomous way. Could you give us some examples, if possible, striking examples, of where this conflict between the behaviour of the army and the position of the government and the Assembly became apparent.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first example was when General Mladic, retired General Subotic, army General Subotic, and the army never came to attend a government meeting. From the beginning of the war, General Ratko Mladic had courteous communication with the government and president of the Assembly, but after that, he didn't even do so on a courteous basis. The General Staff and the army and the leaders of the army, the only relationship they had was with the president of the Republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. And another example that I should like to quote, and I said this a few days ago, what would happen is this: The General Staff, that is to say the army, would, for example, arrest seven or eight ministers and keep them incarcerated for about ten days, and they would feed them like domestic animals, and nobody could say anything about it or do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But were there any open conflicts in terms of the operations of the army, not approved by the government or by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, according to the law governing the army and all laws and by-laws that were enforced, the General Staff did not need to inform either the government or the Assembly about its military actions. Just the Presidency, or rather, the president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but even if they would not have to report, that does not mean automatically that no one was aware of the operations, perhaps not in detail, but ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, but I'm quite sure that the military leaders did not inform anybody within the civilian authorities about their important actions, even the defence minister. If there were some more important operations undertaken by the army, I'm sure they wouldn't have informed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I have to understand your answer to be that, for example, taking over the villages or cities would be something, totally unknown military operations, perhaps, that were not reported or that these things could happen without anyone being aware of it on the higher levels?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant that the General Staff did inform the president of the Republic and Presidency about such operations, but as far as their future operations and actions, I don't know that anybody knew about them except the president. They were -- had a high degree of autonomy and were far superior to the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking specifically about future operations, but also operations that had taken place already and which would not have approved by the Assembly or a majority in the Assembly or by the government or government ministers. I mean by approval that they would not agree with it, even if no formal approval would have been required.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one would know about that? Because my question was that although perhaps not reported, that these things could happen without anyone being aware of it on the higher levels, well, let's say Assembly members or ministers in the government. They would not be aware of matters like gain of certain terrain by the army, including perhaps villages? They would not be aware?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The army did not inform anybody about its activities except their superiors, that is to say, the Presidency and the president. Or perhaps if they considered it necessary for engaging in an operation in a certain area, then part of the police, perhaps, or somebody from the area. That is possible. But they had the right to decide who they were going to inform and who they were not going to inform for each operation, and that was their right, pursuant to the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it also mean that you were not aware of what parts of the territory of the Republic was under Serbian military control?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April onwards, or rather, from April to May, the situation changed, and the minister of defence informed us in the government, or at the assemblies, by the military officials who would report about the situation, the terrain, the deployment of forces, the distribution of the area, and everything else that they considered that parliament and the government should know about. So the defence minister and minister of the interior would report to us on a regular basis about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then were there any -- were there ever any operations or was there ever any result of an operation that you would not agree with?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't give it that much thought when I went to the civilian section of -- I wasn't informed of those activities. It was outside my competence. I had a lot of problems in the civilian section of the legislation and so on, so I didn't have much contact with the army and just on occasion with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to move to another area. You told us about detention facilities under the control of the army. Who had decided which detention facilities were under army control and were there any others not under the army's control? So who determined that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the facilities taken control of by the army came under the army, those taken over by the police were -- there the police was in charge. So depending on the situation on the ground. Nobody determined this in any special way, and divided it up among the army and the police. It was ad hoc from one case to the next and the vast majority were held by the army and a smaller portion was held by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer well that you said this was just a factual matter rather than the result of any decision?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any detention facilities still under the responsibility of the minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during 1992 we tried to take over certain facilities from the police and the army, and I think we succeeded in doing so for a couple of facilities and a couple of prisons. But at the beginning of the war, where people were incarcerated, you saw authority over them being the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how about those persons that were incarcerated already prior to the war, let's say being sentenced for ordinary crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those facilities, as far as the territory of Republika Srpska was concerned, existed in Foca, and that particular facility came under army control. I don't know what actually happened to those people, to the prisoners, but in 1992 we tried to take over that prison. And while I was minister, we were not successful in doing so. And the other prisons were investigative prisons on the territory of Republika Srpska. So the prison where people were serving sentences on the territory of Republika Srpska only existed in Foca, and that was under army control for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were there Serbs detained there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, because the prisons before the war had men and women, Serbs and non-Serbs. They were mixed, a mixed population. And there were prisoners who were serving prison terms of up to ten years. And Zenica was the prison for the grievous crimes on the territory of the Federation. There were three or four enterprises such as Ribnjak, and so on that we used as detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did Serbs detained have to serve their sentences imposed before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware whether it ever happened that Serbs would not have to serve their sentences or were released in order to enable them to join armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but quite possibly the army recruited prisoners for the army and amnestied them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who, then, amnestied them? Did the army do that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did ever a similar thing happen to a non-Serb in detention?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in one of the documents that was shown to you, next to the issue of the unification of the military judiciary and the civilian judiciary, a proposal was mentioned for the postponement of the execution of punishment, and it was added that the positive and the negative aspects should be considered. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was at the Assembly in Zvornik, then yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us what the positive and the negative aspects of the postponement of an execution of punishment is?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for lesser crimes, when there was a food shortage for prisoners, then it was considered that for lesser offences, it was better to release them rather than to hold prisoners in prison when the prevailing conditions were not conducive to a normal life there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I have no further questions for you. Have the questions by the Bench raised any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have a document which at the moment we don't have copies of. It's a very short document. It's in B/C/S. And I'm told, because I wouldn't know any better, I'm told that it is a copy of Mr. Zepinic's resignation. I'm sorry, Mr. Tieger wishes to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I actually thought I recognised -- is that ETSA02-6813?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The very same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any reason to believe that the parties would agree on a fact appearing from that document and wants to convey that to the Chamber or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suspect -- sorry. I suspect that Mr. Stewart wanted to present it to the witness in connection with Judge El Mahdi's questions and just have him confirm whether or not that was the resignation about which they were speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger has just scored two out of two. He was right about the document and he's right about that as well, Your Honour. It's his afternoon so far. So -- but that is correct, that is exactly what I'm about to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If both parties agree that the written letter of resignation was addressed to a certain person, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi would even accept that without putting it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I should still put it in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I should mention also we have an English translation. I don't know if that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could have the English translation perhaps on the ELMO and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was going to invite Ms. Cmeric to read it, but it's such a short letter that if Ms. Cmeric or anybody else concerned more directly with interpretation has no problem with -- of course the booth don't have the original document. It's only a few lines, Your Honour. We're just making sure that we're happy with the translation before we proceed. Further cross-examination by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you've got the letter in your own language, and I'm now reading from a translation. This appears -- well, it's agreed, as I understand it, it is a copy of Mr. Zepinic's letter of resignation. It's addressed to the Assembly of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the attention of Mr. President; subject: resignation letter. "In regard to the agreement on personnel policy, realisation that the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm hereby submitting irrevocable resignation from the function of deputy minister of internal affairs. I'd appreciate it if you'd kindly consider this request at the next Assembly session. Respectfully --" and then although the signature is illegible, probably there wouldn't be any serious suggestion that it wasn't Mr. Zepinic's signature that appeared on that letter. So it appears, would you agree, Mr. Mandic, from this letter perhaps it wasn't that it was Mr. Krajisnik, either personally or as president of the Assembly, whatever precisely that distinction is, it wasn't Mr. Krajisnik himself who had the power to accept or reject the resignation; it went before the Assembly, the request to resign?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've tried to explain to this Honourable Trial Chamber that Mr. Zepinic submitted his resignation directly to the president of the Assembly, whereas ministers can only be granted their request for resignation by the Assembly itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For this purpose, are you counting Mr. Zepinic as a minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain if you've understood this fully. Both the ministers and the deputies were appointed and dismissed from their function by the Assembly, but requests such as this one were submitted to the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, what it comes to is this: It was submitted to the president of the Assembly. We see that. It was addressed to Mr. Krajisnik. The letter itself expressly requests that Mr. Zepinic's letter of resignation -- or his resignation in this letter goes before the Assembly itself; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was exactly my point, Mr. Stewart. That's what I've been trying to explain. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was perfectly clear to me that you said were appointed and dismissed from the functions by the Assembly, but requests were submitted to the president of the Assembly, which is the -- I would say the usual way of addressing a body that you send a letter to. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got to say that it was not, and it was not clear to me, because that wouldn't be the effect of the word "whereas" at line 24 -- at page 24, line 6. The effect of the "whereas" in that sentence is to draw a distinction which absolutely needs clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But if Your Honour is satisfied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The clearness came in line 10. I had the same hesitations on line 6, and it became perfectly clear in line 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, with the utmost respect, I'm very glad it's clear now, but Your Honour it's only caution on behalf of counsel when two apparently contradictory answers have been given to make sure which of them is the evidence and which is correct. But, Your Honour, I'm -- I -- so I make no apology for pursuing it, Your Honour, but I am very happy it is absolutely clear in everybody's and, particularly importantly, the Trial Chamber's minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you were asked a number of questions -- well, first of all, you were asked about instructions in relation to the division of the MUP. You were asked about instructions received from the Assembly, or instructions of the Assembly. This is the position, isn't it, Mr. Mandic - please confirm whether this is correct - that no instructions were given by the Assembly in relation to the division of the MUP except such instructions as are contained only in the form of the published decisions of the Assembly as a legislative organ.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. What I had in mind were the laws precisely, the constitution of Republika Srpska and the law on internal affairs that had been passed by the Assembly and which you yourself presented a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when similarly His Honour Judge El Mahdi put to you that the government followed the directions which came from the Assembly as the representative of the people, that again, the only sense in which the government followed the directions of the Assembly was that it observed such laws and decisions as were publicly made by the Assembly as the legislative organ?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, the government had to put into effect all the decisions taken by the Assembly and abide by the laws passed by the Assembly, which had to do with the work of the government and the ministries. This way, the government would adhere to the enactments passed by the Assembly, that is to say, both the laws and the by-laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to get it clear: Apart from laws passed, decisions publicly taken by the Assembly that have legal force from the legislative body, apart from that, there was no mechanism or instructions to be given by either the Assembly or the president of the Assembly to the government as to what it should do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are fully right, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment? I just need to find a page reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have a keyword, Mr. Stewart, I might be able to assist you, if it is about today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm pretty much -- pretty much there. Thank you. I appreciate the offer of help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you said, and this was at page 15, line 11, you said: "My personal opinion, Your Honour," and this was in answer to questions from His Honour Judge El Mahdi, "is that the party, or rather, the civilian authorities had very little influence on the army, and the army acted independently and exerted its authority as it saw fit." So when you were talking about the civilian authorities that, in your opinion, had very little influence on the army, do you include in "civilian authorities" all the civilian authorities, including the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. That was asked and answered and made quite clear, in fact. That distinction was made, was drawn repeatedly by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it's not asked and answered, Your Honour. It's precisely because the questions and answers might be argued to leave the matter unclear that I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you give us the exact line where the answer was given to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll have to take a moment and scroll back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be allowed to repeat my answer, it might be helpful to both sides in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. An objection against this question, because it would have been answered already. So Mr. Tieger should be able to find a place where you gave the answer and we have the literal text, then, in front of us. Perhaps I'll ask for a clarification of a question I put to the witness myself. Mr. Mandic, upon a question I put to you about conflicts between the government and the Assembly, on the one side, and the army, on the other side, you gave us your first example that they even would not pay a courtesy visit any more to the government. But you said the only relationship there was, was with Dr. Karadzic. What did you mean exactly when you said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be obliged. Could we have the reference, please. It would help us to follow this apparently not absolutely easy area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Page 16, line 10, 11. I'll read it to you, Mr. Mandic. You talked about the first example, General Mladic, and then you said: "General Ratko Mladic had courteous communication with the government and president of the Assembly, but after that, he didn't even do so on a courteous basis." I said visits, but that's not correct. "Of the General Staff and the army and the leaders of the army, the only relationship they had was with the president of the Republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic." So my question was: What exactly did you mean by this relationship? And more specifically, would they listen to him, or was there a conflict as well, or who was in the lead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very difficult, Your Honour, to describe such nuances, but the fact is that the army cooperated solely with the president of the Republic and had respect for him, both as president of the Republic and as commander-in-chief. And if I may help

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Except for the president of the Republic, the army did not cooperate with the civilian authorities. And when I say "civilian authorities," I mean both the government and the parliament, and especially the government. That was an executive branch of government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not Mr. Karadzic, as far as I understand? Yes. You said "except for the president of the Republic." Yes. Your answer is clear. I should have listened better to you. Well, whether or not the question was answered before, at least it's answered now. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Would Your Honour forgive me. I'm just reading, if I may, please, for a moment, something on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm just following on from the answer which I had been quoting to you, Mr. Mandic, before we had these exchanges and then His Honour Judge Orie's question, you had said: "My personal opinion is that the party, or rather, the civilian authorities had very little influence on the army, and the army acted independently and exerted its authority as it saw fit." And then specifically, in answer to His Honour's questions, you said: "The fact is that the army cooperated solely with the president of the Republic," and that's Dr. Karadzic, "and had respect for him, both as president of the Republic and as commander-in-chief." My first question then, Mr. Mandic, is: How much were you in a position to assess the degree of cooperation between the army and the president of the Republic, Dr. Karadzic, from April 1992 over the next four or five months?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as much as a minister in a government could, of course, also based on my knowledge of Mr. Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic, and thanks to the fact that I stayed at Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That doesn't quite indicate the degree of your ability to assess the degree of cooperation. What was it -- were you able closely to follow what degree of cooperation there was between the army and Dr. Karadzic, or moderately, or not very much? I'm just inviting you to see if you can give the Trial Chamber an idea of how much you were able to assess yourself of what you're talking about, which is the degree of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not assess the degree to which I was informed about the relationship between the president of the Republic and the army, but the fact remains that I was there. I was a member of the government. I knew the people. And I've presented my position and views with regard to the relationship between the army and the civilian authorities, and between the army, on the one hand, and the president of the Republic, on the other. And it will be up to the Honourable Trial Chamber to assess the relevance and weight of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said, and the reference here is page 18, line 6 -- Judge Orie asked him - asked you, I'm sorry, Mr. Mandic - Judge Orie asked you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It's -- because Your Honour put a statement and then a question, I'm trying to find a point at which I can present it in a way that is fairly understood by the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His Honour said: "My question was although perhaps not reported, these things," which seems to be military operations, "these things could happen without anyone being aware of it on the higher levels, well, let's say Assembly members or ministers in the government they would not be aware of matters like gain of certain terrain by the army including, perhaps, villages, they would not be aware ..." And your answer was: "No, Your Honour. The army did not inform anybody about its activities except their superiors, that is to say, the Presidency and the president or perhaps if they considered it necessary engaging in an operation in a certain area, then part of the police or somebody from the area." So the part where you say "the army did not inform anybody about its activities except their superiors, that is to say, the Presidency and the president," when you refer to their superiors there as "the Presidency and the president," could you make it clear who it is you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking solely about the president, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and members of the Presidency, Dr. Biljana Plavsic and Dr. Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to leave aside, Mr. Mandic, if you like, legal and definition issues. Is it that from your own observations and knowledge at the time, you knew that the people to whom the army was giving information were Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Plavsic, Dr. Koljevic, and only those three?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my own observations, I can say that they informed only Dr. Karadzic, and their cooperation was a very close one, whereas I think that the army did not really regard the other two members of the Presidency, Dr. Biljana Plavsic and Dr. Nikola Koljevic, too seriously. They were people who were in charge of other spheres of public life and activity in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able, from what you saw yourself, to form an assessment of the degree to which army activities, and I'm talking about the Serb army, army activities in Republika Srpska that were conducted by the military without any reference to any civilian authority, including Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question. You see, the army was stationed at its own positions and did not communicate much with the civilian authorities. I was not really familiar with the specifics of where they were based or what activities they were pursuing. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A different topic, Mr. Mandic. His Honour Judge El Mahdi asked you whether you trusted the information from television, and this was His Honour's phrase, "speaking in the name of the government." Did any of the television channels in those early months of the war purport to speak actually in the name of the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one television, with one channel, and three journalists. We had one minister in charge of information and had one car that was used for the official purposes that we received from Belgrade. The television was a public company, and our channel of communication with the television went through the minister for information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I should clarify my question, Mr. Mandic. I'm not proposing to ask you about perhaps that rather broader, more difficult area of any suggestion of control and so on. It's a simple question: Whether the television channel, in its presentation of its material, whether it presented itself as speaking in the name of the government.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. They were an autonomous public company, and these were mostly people who had used to work for the joint television in Sarajevo. They were very experienced journalists and professionalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm delighted to tell Your Honour that was my last question. So the clock and I are in happy harmony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of questions, and I agree with the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then have a break until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to ask Mr. Registrar to assign a number to the resignation letter of Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm obliged, Your Honour. I mentioned that to Mr. Tieger a moment ago. So that's absolutely right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be number D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D33, and D33.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further examination by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in response to a question asked by the Court, you referred to an incident during which you said seven to eight ministers were arrested by the police -- by the army, excuse me. When do you say that happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but I do know that the incident took place when I was speaking about the relationship between the civilian and military authorities and how much the will of the army depended very little on the civilian authorities. Now, when this actually happened, I really can't remember, but I do know that it was sometime during the war, without specifying a date. And I do know that it was in the Han Pijesak area, or the Romanija area, Mount Romanija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that could have taken place in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very possible, Mr. Tieger, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in connection with the information provided to the president, or the Presidency, by the military: Yesterday we spoke briefly about the minutes of the sessions of the Presidency, and I believe you indicated you hadn't had any opportunity to see such minutes or to be aware of what the minutes reflected about who the members of the Presidency were or how regularly they attended the Presidency meetings.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said, Mr. Tieger, that I was not informed about those minutes and who attended all those meetings. So yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it it would also be true that you would not be aware of whether the minutes of such meetings reflected whether military figures, including members of the Main Staff, briefed the Presidency members on operations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or which members of the Presidency were present when that took place.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't informed of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were military documents directed to your attention in 1992 and 1993, operational reports, combat readiness reports, SIT reports, generalised reporting on events?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be true, then, that you would not be aware of the extent to which such documents reflected that the objectives of planned operations were brought to the attention of the highest leadership of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or the extent to which such documents advised the highest leadership of the outcome of such operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this really seems to be just a series of the same question, when the witness has already said that these documents were not directed to his attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, your questions were very much related to what one could read from those documents that were never addressed to the witness, so I take it that whatever was in those documents, that it would be on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Mandic, Judge El Mahdi directed some questions to you concerning Serbian TV, and the -- your familiarity with what was on Serbian TV and the nature of that programming. And in that connection, I'd like to play one additional intercept and have it marked next in order. That would be intercept dated 18 June 1992 between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Ninkovic, ERN ET03282496. Mr. Mandic, before we begin that intercept, perhaps you can tell us who Mr. Rade Ninkovic was.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
