utterances.text: Yes. Did we already receive that document? And I do understand that the parties do agree, so therefore, the 466 is then admitted into evidence as well. Having dealt with the exhibits, I'd like to move on with a decision on 92 bis witnesses. It's an oral decision, although it will take some time to read it out. This is a decision on two lots of 92 bis witnesses. I briefly recall that the Chamber is seized of two Prosecution motions for the admission of 92 bis evidence. The first was filed on the 6th of June, 2003. That's the so-called 7th motion. And the second was filed on the 9th of January, 2004. That's the 8th motion. The Chamber described the procedural history of the Prosecution's Rule 92 bis applications in its decision of the 7th of April of 2004. There is no reason to repeat it here. I would only add that on the 28th of September, 2004, the parties met with the Chamber's legal officer and agreed to a timetable to deal with the remaining 61 crime base witnesses, in four lots. This decision concerns the first two lots. I would like to emphasise that the Chamber has considered only the material identified by the Prosecution in the annexes to the 7th and the 8th motions and in the list of 92 bis witnesses filed on the 24th of March, 2003. The Chamber has applied the legal standards set out in the decision of the 7th of April, 2004. The Chamber has decided to deliver the present decision orally for reasons of expeditiousness. The parties should be assured that the Chamber considered their submissions in every detail. The Chamber has, as always, checked all the material proposed for admission, even when the Defence did not raise any objection to it. On several occasions, the Prosecution's attention has been drawn to the fact that the information before the Chamber on the protective measures required for its 92 bis witnesses is not complete, and for this witness I shall refer here to witnesses by their "KRAJ" code. I would now ask you, Mr. Registrar, to hand out to the parties a list showing the names of some of the 92 bis witnesses I shall refer to in this decision. The list also shows the witnesses' "KRAJ" code. I draw your attention to the fact that the list you now see contains a blank column for the exhibit number to be assigned to each witness. This shall be done at another time. The Chamber has listed the documentary items that go with each witness. What we propose is that these items be produced by the Prosecutor, in one final version, including the redactions, as we find them in the list, and to be delivered to the registrar in this case. And then, these items then produced will be assigned exhibit or tab identifiers by the registrar at the next housekeeping session. I shall first deal with the witnesses in relation to whom the Defence stated that their evidence may be admitted without cross-examination. These witnesses are: KRAJ 318, KRAJ 026, KRAJ 612, KRAJ 335, KRAJ 562, KRAJ 034, KRAJ 057, KRAJ 051, KRAJ 015, KRAJ 281, KRAJ 133, KRAJ 003, KRAJ 139, KRAJ 141, KRAJ 469, KRAJ 321, KRAJ 148. The evidence of these witnesses, as shown in the hand-out, including the redaction also shown in the hand-out, meets the 92 bis admissibility requirements, and is therefore admitted. The Chamber does not require the appearance of any of these witnesses. In respect of witness KRAJ 051, the Chamber draws the attention of the parties to the fact that it has not followed the Defence's suggestion in relation to one redaction. This proposed redaction, which is shown in the hand-out, was also opposed by the Prosecution. The Chamber has considered whether leaving in this sentence would necessitate calling the witness for cross-examination. The Chamber's conclusion is that there is no need for the witness to appear. I now turn to the witnesses whom the Chamber has decided to call for cross-examination. There are three such witnesses in the two lots we are considering here. Their names and associated materials are not shown in the hand-out. The documents relating to these three witnesses shall be assigned exhibit or tab identifiers and shall be admitted into evidence, subject to any further objections, at the time they are heard in cross-examination. The three witnesses to be called, and I again refer to the "KRAJ" code, for the reasons given before, are: KRAJ 458. The Chamber finds that the proposed evidence of this witness meets the 92 bis admissibility requirements. The Chamber considers that the references to the accused contained in this material cannot be interpreted as relating, in the relevant sense, to the acts or conduct of the accused. The witness's evidence relates to events preceding the alleged takeover of the municipality of Banja Luka; to the operations of the Banja Luka Public Security Station and Security Services Centre (including their reporting procedures to the Ministry of the Interior); and to the activities of the SDS leadership in Banja Luka. In the Chamber's view, the accused should have the opportunity to cross-examine Witness 458 on these issues. KRAJ 063. The Chamber understands that the Prosecution is presently seeking the admission of the transcripts from the Stakic case only. The Chamber finds that the proposed evidence of this witness meets the 92 bis admissibility requirements. The Chamber considers that the references to the accused contained in this material cannot be interpreted as relating, in the relevant sense, to the acts or conduct of the accused. The Chamber sees no reason to admit into evidence any portion of the Stakic transcripts not already highlighted by the Prosecution but may reconsider this position on specific portions of the transcript, once they are identified and explained by the Defence. The Chamber has decided that had it would be appropriate to allow the cross-examination of Witness 063 on a small range of specific topics not related to the witness's crime base evidence. The Defence is invited to inform the Chamber of the specific topics on which it wishes to cross-examine the witness, and the Defence is invited to do so by the 24th of January, 2005. The Prosecution is to await the Chamber's instructions on this point. KRAJ 428. The Chamber admits the statement into evidence, since it meets the requirements of Rule 92 bis. The Chamber allows cross-examination, unless the Prosecution agrees to redact that portion of the statement which situates the accused in a textile factory. The Chamber notes that this portion is hearsay evidence, it is relatively vague, and would need corroboration and further specification to fit it in, in a meaningful way, with the Prosecution's evidence as it has been presented until now. The Prosecution is invited to inform the Chamber of its position on this matter by the 24th of January, 2005. Finally, the parties will recall that the evidence of another witness from the first lot of witnesses, the witness with KRAJ 629, 629 code, was admitted subject to cross-examination by the Chamber's oral decision of the 3rd of November, 2004. The relevant transcript pages being 8032 and 8033. I now turn to the witnesses whose evidence is to be admitted without cross-examination, despite the Defence argument to the contrary. You'll find the names on the list handed out to you by the registrar, and these witnesses are: KRAJ 032, KRAJ 087, KRAJ 652, KRAJ 552, KRAJ 336, KRAJ 341, KRAJ 019, KRAJ 124, KRAJ 029. The Chamber finds that the Defence has failed to establish a sufficient basis to justify cross-examination of these witnesses. Where the proposed material includes transcripts, the Chamber finds that the witnesses were adequately cross-examined in previous proceedings in relation to the subjects mentioned by the Defence. Where the Defence complains of vagueness, imprecision, or hearsay, the Chamber takes the position that, in these specific instances, these purported weaknesses may affect the weight to be given to the evidence but not its admissibility. The Chamber, therefore, conscious of the flaws in the evidence in some respects, admits the evidence of the above-mentioned witnesses, without requiring them to appear for cross-examination. I conclude by noting that the Prosecution recently removed Witness 545, 545, from the viva voce witness list and added him to the 92 bis witness list for Banja Luka. As the Chamber has not received a 92 bis request in relation to this witness, it will not address the parties' submissions until such time as the Prosecution files its request. As for witness with "KRAJ" code 079 from Gacko municipality, the Chamber understands that the Prosecution is still considering what material to propose for admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis. That is the decision on the first two lots of 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the next procedural issue, I invite Judge El Mahdi to address the parties. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor. I would like to make a statement. This is addressed to the parties. This is the statement I wish to make: After having given notice to the Chamber, I wish personally to inform the parties of my decision to withdraw from the present case, a decision which takes effect as from the 14th of January, 2005. I consider that the parties have a right to know the reasons which have brought me to make this decision, and I have to own up, was not easy, but was the only decision which was indispensable to guarantee the best possible way the proceedings -- continuation of the proceedings. As you know, my term of office as a permanent Judge with the International Tribunal is finishing at the end of November 2005. Beyond that date, I do not consider that I'm qualified or mandated by the Statute to continue to sit in the Tribunal. Therefore, taking into account the procedure in which we presently find ourselves, I think it is highly improbable that this case will be finished and the judgement rendered before mid-November. This is the reason why I have taken the decision to withdraw from this case. Aware of the fact that I have to leave the Tribunal before the end of this trial, I have decided, for personal reasons, of professional ethics, and in the interests of justice, to do so now and not to wait at the end of my term of office. This decision is, according to me, the only decision which would allow to be sure that the proceedings will continue in a satisfactory way and that the fundamental rights of Mr. Krajisnik would be respected in a trial so that he can have a fair trial, as guaranteed by the Statute. Before I give back the floor to the President of the Chamber, I wish to express my deep gratitude to the representatives of the parties, to their assistants, teams, as well as to the registrar, the interpreters, and all the staff which has assisted the Chamber. I also wish to convey to all of them, as well as to Mr. Krajisnik, my most sincere wishes for the new year. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge El Mahdi. I would adjourn for a couple of minutes only, and then, upon return, I'd like to address the parties, as the Presiding Judge of this Chamber, under Rule 15 bis. We adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 5.17 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before the break, I would like to address the parties in my capacity as Presiding Judge under Rule 15 bis (C). The Presiding Judge who has to report to the President of the Tribunal. I asked Judge Canivell to accompany me at this very moment, since we may, and I emphasise we may, end up in a situation where we, as two Judges, would have to consider to take a decision under Rule 15 bis (D), a decision to continue the proceedings before this Trial Chamber with a substitute Judge. Therefore, I found it important that Judge Canivell would not miss one single word spoken in relation to the present situation. The Chamber, and I myself, have given some thought on the interpretation of Rule 15 bis (C), and more specifically, on the words "by reason of non-re-election," or as it says a bit further on "for any reason." The question was whether this phrase would include a situation where it is foreseeable that the non-re-election would make the Judge unable to continue sitting in the case until the judgement would be delivered. There is no realistic expectation that a judgement, after both parties have presented their case, will be delivered by the end of the mandate of Judge El Mahdi. It would make no sense, it would not be in the spirit of Rule 15 bis, and would even, in the opinion of the Chamber, go against the interests of the accused and against the interests of justice, if Judge El Mahdi would continue to sit on this case, knowing that it is likely that he would finally not be able to take part in the delivery of the judgement in this case. I said it makes no sense. I said it would be against the spirit of the Rule and go against the interests, and that would be irrespective of whether the Chamber would continue to hear the case with a substitute Judge or whether the case would be reheard entirely. In case of continuing this partly heard case with a substitute Judge, it is of great importance that the new Judge would hear as much of the case as possible, by direct hearing and seeing the evidence that will be presented. Substitution of Judge El Mahdi should therefore, in that scenario, take place at shortest notice. If the case would be reheard on from its beginning, there's no reason to further wait and hear evidence that could never serve the Judges in reaching their decisions. I have discussed the situation as it is now with Judge El Mahdi, and I'm aware of his opinion, his decision, firmly anchored in his conscience and in professional ethics, that due to his non-re-election, he is unable to continue sitting in the Krajisnik case after his present mandate expires, which will be in mid-November 2005. As a consequence, I determined that I am, as a Presiding Judge, now confronted with a situation where a Judge is unable, for reasons of non-re-election, in combination with the "any reasons" clause of Rule 15 bis (C), to continue sitting in this part-heard case for a period which is likely to be longer than of a short duration. Rule 15 bis (C) instructs me to report this situation to the President. Since the presentation of evidence has begun in this case, the President cannot order the continuation of the proceedings with the newly assigned Judge unless the accused has given his consent. I would like to include in my report to the President whether or not the accused gives his consent to continue, and I would like to have a response to that question not later than by next Tuesday. For the parties, I would like to draw your attention to Article 15 bis (D), and perhaps the easiest way of doing that is just to read it out: "If, in the circumstances mentioned in the last sentence of paragraph (C), the accused withholds his consent, the remaining Judges may nonetheless decide to continue the proceedings before a Trial Chamber with a substitute Judge if, taking all the circumstances into account, they determine unanimously that doing so would serve the interests of justice. This decision is subject to appeal directly to a full bench of the Appeals Chamber by either party. If no appeal is taken or the Appeals Chamber affirms the decision of the Trial Chamber, the President shall assign to the existing Bench a Judge who, however, can join the Bench only after he or she has certified that he or she has familiarised himself or herself with the record of the proceedings. Only one substitution under this paragraph may be made." The Chamber has decided that it will not hear any further evidence in this case until all necessary decisions under Rule 15 bis have been taken. In practical terms, this means the following: If the case would be reheard on from the beginning, the case would be scheduled to restart shortly after the effective date of the withdrawal of Judge El Mahdi, which is the 14th of January; therefore, most likely, then, the restart of the case would be either later in week 3 or in week 4 of 2005, starting respectively the 17th and the 24th of January, 2005. If the Chamber would continue to hear the case, whether with or without the consent of the accused, in which latter case the Appeals Chamber might finally have to decide the matter, the newly assigned Judge will have to certify that he or she has familiarised him or herself with the record of the proceedings. I do not expect that such certification may be issued any earlier than in week 6 of 2005, if not later. Only at that point in time, the case may be then continued. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If either party would want to make any submissions at this time in relation to what I just said, they're invited to do so. If not, I would like to hear from -- I should say the accused, because the Rules doesn't say -- the Rules do not say the Defence, but I take it, Mr. Krajisnik, that in the present situation you would consult counsel, because counsel are the ones best able to inform you about all consequences of the present situation. But I'd like to know whether we could receive a written response or whether you and counsel would prefer to give the response to the question I just raised in a court hearing, which would then be scheduled for later next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do, as Mr. Krajisnik's counsel, I do, as Your Honour has indicated, I represent him and speak for him in relation to this matter. And we have, of course, had a brief discussion. But, Your Honour, may I just be permitted to say before that, and I'm sorry, but I understand entirely why it's in the absence of Judge El Mahdi, but Judge El Mahdi will, I hope -- well, I'm sure he will at least read this transcript and have conveyed to him anyway our regret, as the Defence team, that a Judge who has treated us with such enormous professional courtesy and respect throughout the case is retiring, but is retiring from this case. But we recognise that it's entirely consistent with the enormous professional integrity and courtesy of Judge El Mahdi that he is taking this step, and we fully respect and understand the reasons. But we would very much like Judge El Mahdi to know that from the Defence, and also to receive, and I think it is one of those rare occasions, Your Honour, where we are entitled to express our personal views. May we convey our personal good wishes to Judge El Mahdi in this particular respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'll personally take care that all of your words are not only delivered in Judge El Mahdi's chambers but that his attention is specifically drawn to those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And Your Honour, I can also say that I know that our views as to the great courtesy and respect shown by Judge El Mahdi are positively shared by Mr. Krajisnik. I can also say that. But, Your Honour, then moving on from that, may I say that as far as the -- moving immediately, Your Honour, to more absolutely practical matters: Tuesday is not a problem for us, Your Honour, provided that we are, because it's too late to fix it today, provided that we are able to arrange sufficient time to see Mr. Krajisnik. It's unusual for there to be a difficulty about that. Just occasionally recently there has been. It may be, Your Honour, that, in view of the importance of the matter, that if there is any such difficulty, perhaps we may appeal to anybody who is able to help us cut our way through any such difficulty. We've had a brief discussion with Mr. Krajisnik. Of course it's a matter, the complexities of the Rule and the various permutations are a matter that we would want to sit down and talk to Mr. Krajisnik more fully, as Your Honour will of course -- Your Honours will appreciate. But, Your Honour, I say no more than that. So far as we -- except that I -- it's probably, whatever step is taken, for the record, it's probably a good idea if we submit it in writing. But, Your Honour, may we, with respect, suggest that whether a court hearing is required in relation to such matter is perhaps a bridge that might be crossed at some point over the next few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll then leave it to you, Mr. Stewart, to inform the Chamber on whether there would be any need of a hearing. Of course, the most important matter is whether consent is given or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I then can report that to the President. It needs no reasons to be given for that. It's entirely up for the accused to make up his mind and to decide that. If for any other reason you would consider it necessary to listen to any other submissions in relation to this issue, I'm quite willing to schedule a hearing for that. But then I'll wait until you've indicated that you would like to have an oral hearing rather than to send a written answer to the question I put.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Very much obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, let me first -- I'll give you an opportunity to say something. Is there any need -- would the Prosecution like to make any submission at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There is nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik, did I -- when looking somewhere else, did I understand that you would like to address me, as Presiding Judge, accompanied by Judge Canivell, at this moment? Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that Judge El Mahdi would be present with us here, that he would return to the courtroom. But as I understand that he will not return, then I should like to say a few words. I should like to ask you to convey to Judge El Mahdi my gratitude for his having followed this trial as closely as he has. This is not just by way of courtesy. My gratitude by way of courtesy. I had the pleasure of listening to his questions and how much attention he paid to listening to the trial and his endeavour to arrive at the truth. As he is no longer a judge, I wish him all the best and good health for his future. Now, I have something unusual to ask you at this point. I am a conservative man and I find it very difficult when people leave, people whom I have -- if I can say so, been associating for some time, to see them leave. Is it customary, or rather, can I send Judge El Mahdi a small gift as a courtesy? Because he was always very attentive to the trial. But if that is not in order, then I apologise for having brought it up. Now, as far as the proposal made by Mr. Stewart, I share his opinions and we shall, of course, confer and provide you with an answer in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. You asked me whether it was customary to give a gift. I can answer that question with a clear "no." I even would say that it's not only not customary, but there are several reasons one could think of why it should not be done. I invite you to discuss the matter with counsel and then to finally make up your mind. What I heard between the lines you've spoken, however, and I think that's also expressed in your question to me whether a gift would be customary or not, is the sincerity of what you expressed, your gratitude, your appreciation for how Judge El Mahdi served and will continue to serve until the 14th of January in this case. And apart from that, the words in writing will reach him. I'll not only, as I promised to Mr. Stewart, personally look at it that he doesn't only receive them but that his attention will also be drawn to that, and I'll add to that, as my personal impression, that this impression was that you spoke those words with great sincerity, from your heart. Then I think we have dealt with the procedural issue, although it is perhaps a bit poor to just call it a procedural issue. We'll adjourn, either until next Tuesday, at a time and a courtroom to be announced later, or until somewhere in January; I cannot tell the parties when exactly.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.46 p.m.,
